intro: Japanese uses two kana syllabaries side by side: hiragana (ひらがな) for native words and grammar, and katakana (カタカナ) for foreign loanwords. Words are usually written together with kanji — the Chinese characters shown beside the example words.

dakuten.label: Dakuten & Handakuten
dakuten.blurb: Add ゛ to voice a sound, or ゜ to turn the h-row into p.

yoon.label: Yōon — contracted
yoon.blurb: A kana plus a small ゃ / ゅ / ょ, blended into one beat.

special.label: Special combinations
special.blurb: Modern katakana blends for borrowed foreign sounds.

sokuon.label: Sokuon — the small tsu
sokuon.blurb: A small っ / ッ that doubles the next consonant.

letters.name: small tsu
letters.memoryTrick: A small っ (half-size つ) doesn't make a sound of its own — it doubles the next consonant and adds a tiny pause, like the catch in 'oops!'. Written full-size it's つ 'tsu'; small, it's the sokuon.

letters.name: small tsu
letters.memoryTrick: The katakana sokuon — a small ッ that doubles the next consonant, common in loanwords. Full-size it's ツ 'tsu'; small, it just lengthens the stop.
